14.s: Which one of the following writs can be issued by a High Court to secure the liberty of the individual?
14.x: Article 226 of the Indian Constitution provides for the power of the High Courts to issue certain writs. To secure the personal liberty of the individual, the High Court can issue a writ of Habeas Corpus. The writ is issued by the Court, whose object is to secure the release of a person found to be detained illegally and secure the liberty of the individual. The Supreme Court also has the power to issue writs under Article 32 of Indian Constitution for the enforcement of rights enumerated in Part III of the Constitution, i.e., Fundamental Rights whereas the High Court can also issue writs related to legal rights.

14.s: Which among the following is issued when the procedure is pending in court?
14.x: The writ of Prohibition is issued when the procedure is pending in Court. When the lower court hears any case out of its Jurisdiction, then the upper Court takes over the case by issuing a Prohibition writ.

14.s: The Writ of Certiorari is issued by a Superior Court
o: To an inferior court to transfer the record of
To an inferior court to stop further proceedings in a
To an officer to show his right to hold a particular
To a public authority to produce a person detained by
14.x: The writ of Certiorari is issued to a lower court directing that the record of a particular case be sent up for review, together with all supporting files, evidence, and documents, usually with the intention of overruling the judgment of the lower Court. It is one of the mechanisms by which the fundamental rights of the citizens are protected.

14.s: The writ which may be filed for protection of right to Personal Freedom is -
14.x: The word ‘Habeas Corpus’ literally means ‘to have the body of.’ By this writ, the court secures the body of a person who has been imprisoned or detained to be brought before the court to obtain knowledge of the reason or grounds for such detention and to do justice. This writ secures the right of personal liberty.

14.s: A Writ of Prohibition is an order issued by the Supreme Court or High Courts to :
o: a government officer prohibiting him from taking a
the Parliament / Legislative Assembly to pass a law
the lower court prohibiting continuation of proceedings
the Government prohibiting it from following an
14.x: The Writ of Prohibition is a legal term that implies "to prohibit, prevent, forbid, or restrain". It is a legal remedy that can be sought from a higher court to prevent a lower court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction or acting unlawfully. It is a command issued by a superior court to a lower court, directing it to cease proceedings that are beyond its legal authority or contrary to the principles of natural justice. In essence, the writ of prohibition serves as a check on the power of lower courts or tribunals, ensuring that they operate within the boundaries of their jurisdiction and adhere to the principles of justice. It acts as a mechanism to correct errors and prevent potential harm that may arise from biased or unfair proceedings. It cannot be enforced against administrative agencies, statutory authorities, or private persons or enterprises. It is exclusively applicable to judicial and quasi-judicial bodies. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

14.s: Regarding the Habeas Corpus, choose the WRONG answer.
o: It is a writ for personal liberty
A petition of Habeas Corpus lies against the executive authority, not available against private individuals
It can be issued by the Supreme Court and High Courts
It orders production of the detained person before the court
14.x: The writ of Habeas Corpus protects personal liberty by requiring authorities to produce a detained person before a court. Contrary to the incorrect statement, the writ can be issued not only against government authorities but also against private individuals who illegally detain someone.

14.s: Which one of the following writs is regarded as the greatest safeguard for the liberty of a person?
14.x: The Writ of Habeas Corpus is regarded as the greatest safeguard of the liberty of a person. It calls upon the person who has detained another to produce the latter before the court, to let the court know on what grounds he has been confined, and to set him free if there is no legal justification for the imprisonment.

14.s: Under which Article of the Constitution of India Supreme Court safeguards the Fundamental Rights of the Indian citizens?
14.x: Article 32 of the Indian Constitution is the “Right to Constitutional Remedies” for the enforcement of rights conferred by Part III, i.e., Fundamental Rights. The Supreme Court has the power to issue directions, orders or writs to safeguard the Fundamental Rights.

14.s: Which of the following cases comes under the Jurisdiction of High Court and Supreme Court?
o: Dispute between the Centre and States
Protection from violation of the Constitution
14.x: The protection/enforcement of Fundamental Rights is a subject that comes under the jurisdiction of both the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Article 226). The High Courts have broader writ jurisdiction under Article 226 than the Supreme Court's Jurisdiction under Article 32. The High Courts can issue writs under Article 226 for the enforcement of fundamental rights and other constitutional rights and for other purposes.

14.s: The Guardian of Fundamental Rights is
14.x: The Constitution of India has assigned Judiciary, i.e. the Supreme Court of India and the High Courts, the responsibility of protecting of fundamental rights. The most significant of fundamental rights is the exclusive right to the constitutional remedies under Art. 32 (High Courts' jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India). Thus, the Guardian of fundamental rights is the Judiciary.

14.s: Which one of the following statements is not correct?
o: K.M. Munshi was one of the members of the drafting
The Constitution of India was adopted by the
The Panchayati Raj was recommended by Balwant
The President of India is the Guardian of Fundamental
14.x: All the given statements are correct, except (d), as the Judiciary (The Supreme Court and the High Courts) is the guardian of fundamental rights, not the President.

14.s: Which of the following rights can be enforced under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution?
14.x: Article 32 of the Constitution provides constitutional remedies against the violation or transgression of fundamental rights, conferred by Part III. The Supreme Court shall have the power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs like Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part-III. That is why the Supreme Court has been called the Guardian of Fundamental Rights.

14.s: Under the Indian Constitution who is the guardian of the fundamental rights?
Which one of the following is regarded as the protector of fundamental rights of citizens and Guardian of the Constitution of India?
14.x: The Supreme Court of India is the protector of the fundamental rights of citizens and the Guardian of the Constitution of India because, through the right to constitutional remedies (Art. 32), it protects the fundamental rights of citizens. Besides, it interprets as well as enforces the provisions of the Constitution.

14.s: Under the Indian Constitution who amongst the following is considered to be the guardian of the fundamental rights?
Which of the following is given the power to enforce the Fundamental Rights by the Constitution?
o: The Supreme Court and High Courts
14.x: Article 13 of the Constitution grants the power of Judicial Review to the Supreme Court, and High Courts in the case of a violation of the Fundamental Rights. The Supreme Court (Art.32) and High Court (Art.226) in exercising their power, may declare any law or enactment passed by the Legislature, void or unconstitutional, on the ground of contravention of the Fundamental Rights.

14.s: Who was the Chief Justice of India when public interest litigation (PIL) was introduced to the Indian Judicial System?
14.x: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) emerged in the late 1970s and early 1980s as a tool to make justice accessible to the poor and marginalised. Justice P.N. Bhagwati, along with Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer, played a pioneering role in liberalising the concept of locus standi. During his tenure as Chief Justice of India (1985–1986), PIL became firmly institutionalised in the Indian judicial system.

14.s:
Consider the following statements:
Assertion (A): Dr. Ambedkar had described Article 32 of the Constitution as the very soul of it. Reason (R) : Article 32 provides an effective remedy against the violation of fundamental rights.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
o: (A) and (R) both are true, and (R) is the correct
(A) and (R) both are true, but (R) is not the correct
14.x: Dr. Ambedkar had described Article 32 as “the very soul and the heart of the Constitution” as Article 32 provides an effective remedy against the violation of fundamental rights enshrined in the Indian Constitution. The Supreme Court has the power to issue directions, orders or writs for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights. Thus, (A) and (R) both are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

14.s:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : The Supreme Court of India has exclusive jurisdiction regarding Constitutional Validity of Central laws.
Reason (R) : The Supreme court is the Guardian of the India Constitution.
Select the correct answer from the codes given below:
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct expla-
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct
14.x: The High Courts of States also have jurisdiction regarding the Constitutional validity of central laws. The Supreme Court (under Article 32) and the High Courts (under Article 226) can issue writs to protect the fundamental rights of the people. Hence, the Supreme Court does not have exclusive jurisdiction in this case. The Supreme Court is the custodian or the Guardian of the Constitution of India. UPPSC has considered option (a) as the correct one, which is wrong.

14.s:
Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India have been declared by the Supreme Court as the ‘Inviolable basic structure’ of the Constitution:
Select the correct answer from the code given below:
1. Article 32
2. Article 226
3. Article 227
4. Article 245
14.x: A Larger Bench of thirteen Judges in the Kesavananda Bharati Case unequivocally declared that the power of judicial review over legislative action vested in the High Courts under Article 226 and in the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution is an integral and essential feature of the Constitution, constituting part of its basic structure. Article 227 defines; that every High Court shall have superintendence over all courts and tribunals throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises Jurisdiction. These three Articles were declared the inviolable basic structure of the Constitution of India in the Kesavananda Bharati Case.

14.s:
Consider the following statements and select the correct answer from the code given:
Assertion (A) : High Courts are in better position to protect rights of Indian citizens than the Supreme Court.
Reason (R) : Supreme Court can issue writs to protect only Fundamental Rights.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not a correct
14.x: Both the statements are correct. According to Article 32, the Supreme Court can issue writs only for the protection of fundamental rights, but according to Article 226, the High Court can issue writs not only in matters relating to fundamental rights but also in any other matter.

14.s: The power of High Court to issue writ covers:
14.x: The power to issue writs is given to the Supreme Court under Article 32 and the High Court under Article 226 to issue a writ of Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari. The power of the Supreme Court to issue writs is limited to Part III of the Constitution, but the High Court has the right to issue writs for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred in Part III and for any other purpose (Legal Rights).

15.s:
Consider the following statements about Directive Principles: basics:
1. The immediate constitutional model for India's Directive Principles was the Constitution of Ireland (1937).
2. The Instrument of Instructions, an antecedent of the Directive Principles, was found under the Government of India Act, 1919.
3. The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in Part III of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x:
Statement 1: Correct: India took the idea from the Irish Constitution of 1937, which had copied it from the Spanish Constitution.
Statement 2: Incorrect: the Instrument of Instructions was under the Government of India Act, 1935, not 1919.
Statement 3: Incorrect: the DPSPs are in Part IV (Articles 36-51), not Part III.

15.s:
Consider the following statements about Directive Principles: basics:
1. The Directive Principles are referred to as the 'Instrument of Instructions' and the 'Conscience of the Constitution'.
2. The Directive Principles of State Policy aim to establish social and economic democracy and a welfare state.
3. Article 36 of the Constitution deals with the application of the Directive Principles of State Policy.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x:
Statement 1: Correct: DPSP are called the 'Instrument of Instructions' and the 'conscience of the Constitution' (Granville Austin).
Statement 2: Correct: the DPSPs aim at social democracy, economic democracy and a welfare state.
Statement 3: Incorrect: Article 36 defines 'State' for Part IV; Article 37 makes DPSP non-justiciable.

15.s:
Consider the following statements about Directive Principles of State Policy:
1. The sanction behind the Directive Principles is legal.
2. A living wage and promotion of cottage industries are directed by Article 43.
3. The Ninth Schedule was introduced by the First Amendment, 1951.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: DPSPs carry a moral and political sanction; it is FRs that carry a legal sanction.
Statement 2: Correct: Article 43 covers a living wage and cottage industries.
Statement 3: Correct: the First Amendment, 1951 introduced the Ninth Schedule and Articles 31A and 31B.

15.s: Which of the following pairs (Article – Directive) is wrongly matched?
o: Article 49 – Protection of monuments and places of national importance
Article 48 – Agriculture and animal husbandry on scientific lines
Article 47 – Prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs
15.x: Article 50 directs separation of the judiciary from the executive; international peace and security is Article 51.
xa: ⚠ **48** is both **Gandhian** and **Liberal-intellectual**.
**48A** (environment) added by the **42nd, 1976**.
Heritage link: **Art. 49** and FD **51A(f)**.

15.s:
Consider the following statements about classification of Directive Principles:
1. The organisation of village panchayats is directed by Article 39A.
2. Articles 40, 43, 43B and 46 are all generally classified as Gandhian principles.
3. Article 50 is a liberal-intellectual Directive Principle rather than a Gandhian one.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: village panchayats are covered by Article 40; Article 39A is free legal aid.
Statement 2: Correct: Articles 40, 43, 43B and 46 are generally included among Gandhian principles.
Statement 3: Correct: Article 50 (separation of judiciary) is liberal-intellectual; Articles 40, 43B, 46 and 48 are Gandhian.

15.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the classification of Directive Principles is correct?
o: The Constitution expressly divides them into Socialist, Gandhian and Liberal-intellectual categories.
The classification was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment.
The classification into Socialist, Gandhian and Liberal-intellectual principles is an academic arrangement.
The Supreme Court alone has classified them into three categories in Part IV.
15.x: The Constitution does not itself classify the Directive Principles. The classification into Socialist, Gandhian and Liberal-intellectual categories is an academic arrangement used for study.
15.tq: Distinguish constitutional text from an academic classification.
xs: The **Socialist, Gandhian, Liberal-intellectual** classification is an **academic** grouping — option **(3)**.
The **Constitution itself does not classify** them — options (1), (2), (4) wrong.
xa: ⚠ **43** and **47** are both Socialist and Gandhian; **48** both Gandhian and Liberal-intellectual.
**43B** is classed as **Gandhian**.

15.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Equal justice and free legal aid – Article 39A
15.x: Article 39A provides for equal justice and free legal aid. Humane conditions of work are Article 42, the Uniform Civil Code is Article 44 and environment protection is Article 48A.
n: Article 39A provides equal justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 39A provides free legal aid. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]

Article 44 concerns a Uniform Civil Code. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]

Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?

n: Liberal-Intellectual Principles comprise 7 articles. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]

15.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Directive Principles is incorrect?
o: Article 48A provides for the separation of the Judiciary from the Executive.
Article 50 deals with the separation of the Judiciary from the Executive.
Article 44 deals with the Uniform Civil Code.
Article 39A provides for equal justice and free legal aid.
15.x: A is incorrect: Article 48A is about protecting and improving the environment, forests and wildlife; separation of the judiciary from the executive is Article 50. Articles 44 (UCC) and 39A (free legal aid) are stated correctly.
15.tq: Check the Article number against its subject.
n: Article 39A provides for equal justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 39A provides for free legal aid. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 44 provides for a Uniform Civil Code. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 48A provides for the protection and improvement of the environment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]

The Uniform Civil Code is provided under Article 44 and is still not fully implemented. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Free legal aid is provided under Article 39A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Environmental protection is provided under Article 48A as a Directive Principle. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **Article 48A provides for the separation of the Judiciary from the Executive** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 48A** is to **protect and improve the environment** and safeguard **forests and wildlife**.
**Separation of the Judiciary from the Executive** is **Article 50**; **44** = **UCC**; **39A** = **free legal aid** — all correct.
xa: **48A** was added by the **42nd Amendment**.
The matching Fundamental Duty for environment is **Article 51A(g)**.
**Art. 49** = protection of **monuments and places of national importance**.

15.s: Which of the following pairs (Article – Directive) is wrongly matched?
o: Article 47 – Prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs
Article 46 – Prohibition of the slaughter of cows and calves
15.x: Article 46 promotes the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections; the cow-slaughter ban is Article 48.
n: Article 43 directs the State to promote cottage industries. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]

Article 46 directs the State to promote the economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]

15.s: Which of the following pairs (Article – Directive) is wrongly matched?
o: Article 45 – Originally, free and compulsory education up to 14 years
Article 48 – Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
Article 48A – Safeguarding of forests and wildlife
15.x: Article 49 concerns protection of monuments and places of national importance; the Uniform Civil Code is Article 44.
n: Article 45 originally provided for free and compulsory education up to 14 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 48 provides for the organisation of agriculture. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 48 provides for the organisation of animal husbandry. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 48A provides for safeguarding forests and wildlife. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 49 provides for the protection of monuments of national importance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]

15.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections — Article 46
15.x: C is correct: Article 46 protects the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections. The others are mismatched: village panchayats are Art. 40 (not 43), cottage industries are Art. 43 (not 40), and prohibition of intoxicating drinks is Art. 47 (not 48).
15.tq: Start from the sure Article–subject pair and eliminate the shifted numbers.
xs: **Art. 46** — interests of **SCs, STs and weaker sections** — option **(3)**.
Protection of weaker sections is a DPSP only — **not an FD**.

15.s: Which one of the following is included in the Directive Principles of State Policy?
o: Protection in respect of conviction for offences
Protection of life and personal liberty
Equal pay for equal work for both men and women

15.s:
Consider the following statements about Directive Principles: Articles 38-39:
1. Courts have generally used the Directive Principles as interpretive aids, including in reading certain principles into Article 21.
2. The Directive Principle relating to a social order based on social, economic and political justice and the minimisation of inequalities is contained in Article 38.
3. Article 39(a) directs the State to secure adequate means of livelihood for men and women equally.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x:
Statement 1: Correct: although not independently enforceable, DPSPs are used by courts as interpretive aids, and several have been read into Article 21.
Statement 2: Correct: Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order informed by justice and to minimise inequalities.
Statement 3: Correct: Article 39(a) covers adequate means of livelihood for men and women equally; equal pay is in Article 39(d).

15.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 39 clauses:
1. The protection of children against exploitation and moral or material abandonment, along with development in freedom and dignity, is provided under Article 39(d).
2. Equal pay for equal work for men and women is provided in Article 39(d).
3. Article 39(b) concerns the protection of monuments and Article 39(c) the promotion of international peace.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: this is provided under Article 39(f), not 39(d); its present wording came through the 42nd Amendment.
Statement 2: Correct: Article 39(d) deals with equal pay; 39(e) protects the health and strength of workers and children.
Statement 3: Incorrect: Article 39(b) concerns distribution of material resources of the community for the common good, and 39(c) prevention of concentration of wealth and means of production.

15.s: Which one of the following correctly matches the constitutional provision with its nature?
o: Article 24 — Directive Principle of State Policy
Article 39(f) — Directive Principle of State Policy
Article 21A — Directive Principle of State Policy
15.x: Article 39(f) is a Directive Principle of State Policy. Articles 24 and 21A are Fundamental Rights, while Article 39(e) is also a Directive Principle.
15.tq: Use the Fundamental Right–DPSP distinction to eliminate swapped classifications.
xs: **Art. 39(f)** is a **Directive Principle of State Policy** — option **(3)**.
**39(e)** is also a DPSP, not a Fundamental Right — option (2) wrong.
**Art. 21A** (education 6-14) is a **Fundamental Right** — option (4) wrong.
xa: 39(f) was added by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
**Art. 21A** came with the **86th Amendment (2002)**.

15.s:
Consider the following statements about Directive Principles and related Articles:
1. After the constitutional changes relating to education, Article 45 directs the State to provide early childhood care and education for children below six years of age.
2. Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief are directed by Article 42.
3. Article 350B provides for a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Article 45 covers early childhood care and education until age six; Article 21A is the Fundamental Right to education for ages six to fourteen.
Statement 2: Correct: Article 42 covers humane conditions of work and maternity relief; Article 41 is the right to work.
Statement 3: Correct: the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities is under Article 350B; Article 350A concerns mother-tongue education.

15.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Article 43 provides for a living wage and a decent standard of life.
Article 47 directs the State to raise the level of nutrition, raise the standard of living and improve public health.
Article 43A directs the State to provide for the participation of workers in the management of agriculture.
Article 43A provides for the participation of workers in the management of industries.
15.x: C is incorrect: Article 43A provides for workers' participation in the management of industries, not agriculture. Articles 43 (living wage) and 47 (nutrition, public health) are stated correctly.
15.tq: Watch for one word changed in a provision.
n: Article 43 provides for a living wage. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 43 provides for a decent standard of life. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 43A provides for the participation of workers in the management of industries. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 47 directs the State to raise the level of nutrition. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 47 directs the State to raise the standard of living. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 47 directs the State to improve public health. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
xs: The incorrect statement is that Article 43A provides workers' participation in **management of agriculture** — option **(3)**.
**Article 43A** provides **workers' participation in management** of **industries**, added by the **42nd Amendment**.
**Art. 43** (**living wage**, decent standard of life) and **Art. 47** (**nutrition**, **public health**) are stated correctly.
xa: **Art. 48** covers organisation of **agriculture** and **animal husbandry** on scientific lines.
**Art. 47** also directs **prohibition** of **intoxicating drinks and drugs**.
**Art. 43B** (**co-operative societies**) came with the **97th Amendment**.

15.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 21A provides the Right to Education.
2. Article 44 concerns improvement of nutrition.
3. Article 39(f) concerns the development of children.
Which of the above statements are correct?
15.x: Article 21A is the Right to Education and Article 39(f) concerns child development. Statement 2 is wrong: Article 44 is the Uniform Civil Code; nutrition is Article 47.
n: Article 21A provides the right to education. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 36-39]
Article 24 prohibits child labour. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 36-39]
Article 44 provides for a Uniform Civil Code. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 36-39]
Article 39(f) provides for child development. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 36-39]
Article 47 provides for nutrition improvement. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 36-39]
xa: **Art. 39(e)** = **protection from exploitation**.
**Art. 45** = **early childhood care and education**.
**Art. 44** concerns **marriage** and **family**.

15.s:
Consider the following statements about Directive Principles and amendments:
1. After the 86th Amendment, Article 45 concerns early childhood care and education until six years.
2. Article 47 is a Directive Principle grouped under the Gandhian, not the Socialist, principles.
3. Article 38(2), on minimisation of inequalities, was not added to the Directive Principles by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Article 45 now covers early childhood care and education until age six; education for ages 6-14 is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A.

Fundamental Duties *The Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution are inspired by the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR. *These were added on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee through the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976. *This amendment added a new part (Part IV A) which consists of only one article, that is, Article 51 A. *Presently, the number of Fundamental Duties, as per the Article 51 A, is 11, whereas originally, at the time of its inclusion in the Constitution, the number was 10. 16.x: In the State of Madras Vs Champakam Dorairajan (1951) case, the Supreme Court of India held that, in the case of conflict between these two, the fundamental right shall prevail over the Directive Principles of State policy. It is notable that the state of Madras issued orders for community-based reservation for Medical College seats, in the furtherance of Article 46 of the Directive Principles of State Policy. The said order was challenged on the grounds of violation of fundamental rights under Article 15(1) and Article 29(2). The Supreme Court in its decision, hailed the superiority of the fundamental rights over the directive principles and cancelled the Madras government’s order of community based reservation. To remove the effect of this decision the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 added clause (4) to the Article 15 under fundamental rights. This clause (4) of Article 15 established that, nothing in Article 15 or clause (2) of Article 29 shall prevent the state from making any provision for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

17.x: Rights and duties are interdependent. For every right guaranteed to citizens, there is a corresponding duty. For example, the right to freedom of speech comes with the duty not to misuse this freedom to harm others or disrupt public order. This relationship ensures responsible citizenship and societal balance, as duties help protect and realize the rights of individuals while promoting the common good.

17.x: In the context of India, Rights and Duties are correlative. According to Holland, every right implies the active or passive forbearance by others of the wishes of the party having the right. The forbearance on the part of others is called a duty. Rights and duties are two faces of the same thing. The Supreme Court has observed that there may be a rule which imposes an obligation on an individual or authority and yet it may not be enforceable in a court of law and, therefore, not give rise to a corresponding enforceable right to another person. But it would still be a legal rule because it prescribes a norm of conduct to be followed by such an individual or authority. Thus, rights and duties are correlative, and they give the effect to each other.

17.tq: Reject the absolute-priority trap while retaining the limited interpretive role of duties.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.

n: Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan reaffirmed Parliament’s power to amend any part of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan held that Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Golaknath v. State of Punjab held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]

Minerva Mills v. Union of India restored the balance between Part III and Part IV. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xs: Statements **I and II** are correct — so option **(2) I and II only** is correct.
I: **Golaknath (1967)** held Parliament **cannot** abridge or take away any FR.

18.x: The Supreme Court of India examined the concept of the "Basic structure" of the constitution for the first time in Kesavananda Bharti v. State of Kerala in 1973. Significantly, the Supreme Court reversed its decision in the Golak Nath case in this instance. It declared that Parliament has the authority to restrict or eliminate any of the Fundamental Rights and confirmed the legality of the 24th Constitution Amendment Act. It also established a new theory regarding the "basic structure" or "basic features" of the Constitution. It decided that Parliament could not change the "basic structure" of the Constitution using its constituent power under Article 368. This implies that a Fundamental Right that is a component of the Constitution's "basic structure" cannot be restricted or eliminated by the Parliament.

Again in the Keshvananda Bharati case 1973, the Supreme Court held that the amendment power of the Parliament is wide enough but not unlimited. It may amend fundamental rights but not in such a way as to destroy the Basic Structure of the Constitution. This case outlined the power of the parliament to amend the fundamental rights without destroying the basic structure of the Constitution.

3. Article 43B was inserted into the Directive Principles of State Policy by the 97th Constitutional Amendment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
20.x:
Statement 1: Correct: the 106th Amendment, enacted in 2023, is the latest enacted amendment, not the 105th of 2021.
Statement 2: Correct: Part IXB (Articles 243ZH-243ZT) was struck down for State co-operatives as State ratification was absent.
Statement 3: Correct: Article 43B was inserted to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operatives.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about recent amendments and Bills:
1. In Rajendra N. Shah v. Union of India (2021), Part IXB was held inapplicable to State co-operative societies mainly because it violated Article 19(1)(c).
2. Article 82A is proposed to be inserted by the 129th Constitutional Amendment Bill, 2024.
3. The 130th Constitutional Amendment Bill, 2025 concerns removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Ministers detained for 30 consecutive days on serious charges.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
20.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: it was struck down because the required ratification by the States had not been obtained.
Statement 2: Correct: the 129th Amendment Bill proposes Article 82A and amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327 for simultaneous elections.
Statement 3: Correct: the 130th Amendment Bill concerns such removal and involves Articles 75, 164 and 239AA.

20.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the 106th Constitutional Amendment?
o: It has been criticised for not providing a separate sub-quota for BC women
Southern States fear their share may decline after delimitation
It has already been implemented in all State Legislative Assemblies
It provides one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies
20.x: The women's quota under the 106th Amendment remains unimplemented.
xa: The LoP asked why the **2023** law was tied to **delimitation** (Aug **2026**).
Local bodies: one-third for women since **1992** (**Arts. 243D, 243T**).

20.s: Since 1992, one-third reservation for women in Panchayats and Municipalities has been provided under Articles:
20.x: Articles 243D and 243T deal with reservation in Panchayats and Municipalities respectively, giving women one-third seats since 1992.
xa: The **106th (2023)** extends **one-third seats for women** to legislatures — still **unimplemented**.
Criticism: **no BC sub-quota** in the 106th.

21.s:
Consider the following statements about the basic structure doctrine:
1. H.M. Seervai argued in India in 1965 that the amending power has implied limitations, drawing upon Germany's Basic Law.
2. Justice Mudholkar's dissent in Sajjan Singh first referred to the idea of 'basic features' of the Constitution.
3. Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to review on the basis of the basic structure.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: it was German jurist Dietrich Conrad, not H.M. Seervai, who made this argument in 1965.
Statement 2: Correct: Justice Mudholkar's dissent in Sajjan Singh (1965) is noted as the first judicial reference to basic features.
Statement 3: Correct: Waman Rao used 24 April 1973 as the cut-off; later entries are open to basic-structure review.

21.s:
Consider the following statements about evolution of the basic structure:
1. The Golaknath case (1967) did not hold that a constitutional amendment is 'law' under Article 13.
2. Kesavananda Bharati first propounded the basic structure doctrine and overruled Golaknath.
3. The basic structure doctrine was applied for the first time, with free and fair elections treated as a basic feature, in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: the claim that is not correct about Golaknath is that it arose from a challenge to the 24th Amendment; it challenged the 17th Amendment.
Statement 2: Correct: Kesavananda Bharati propounded the doctrine, overruled Golaknath and upheld the 24th Amendment.
Statement 3: Correct: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) first applied the doctrine and struck down the relevant clause of the 39th Amendment.

21.s: Which one of the following statements about Kesavananda Bharati is correct?
o: It was decided on 26 January 1975 by a 13-judge bench by a 6:7 majority
It was decided by a 7-judge bench by a 6:5 majority in 1971
It was decided on 24 April 1973 by a 13-judge bench by a 7:6 majority
It was decided by an 11-judge bench by a unanimous decision in 1973
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati was decided on 24 April 1973 by a 13-judge bench with a 7:6 majority.
21.tq: Discriminate among closely related dates, bench sizes and majority figures.
xs: **Kesavananda Bharati** was decided on **24 April 1973** by a **13-judge bench**, **7:6** — option **(3)**.
The **13-judge bench** is the **largest bench ever**, headed by CJI **S.M. Sikri**.
The **11-judge bench** (6:5) belongs to **Golaknath (1967)**, not Kesavananda.
xa: **24 April 1973** became the **Waman Rao** cut-off for Ninth Schedule laws.
Kesavananda **overruled Golaknath** and **upheld the 24th Amendment**.
It held the **Preamble is part of the Constitution**.

21.s:
Consider the following statements about amendments and the basic structure:
1. Articles 368(4) and 368(5), and the widened Article 31C, introduced or widened by the 42nd Amendment, were struck down in Minerva Mills.
2. The Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act in 2015 by a majority of 4:1.
3. The insertion of Article 31C was not associated with the First Amendment Act, 1951.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Minerva Mills struck down Articles 368(4) and 368(5) along with the widened form of Article 31C.
Statement 2: Correct: the NJAC case was decided 4:1, treating judicial independence as part of the basic structure.
Statement 3: Correct: Article 31C was inserted by the Twenty-Fifth Amendment Act, 1971.

21.s: Which one of the following statements about the Ninth Schedule is correct?
o: It contains only laws implementing Article 39(b) and Article 39(c).
It contains fewer than 50 entries and enjoys complete immunity from judicial review.
It has grown to more than 280 entries, but inclusion does not confer blanket immunity from judicial review.
It has grown to more than 280 entries, and its contents have no constitutional relationship with Fundamental Rights.
21.x: The Ninth Schedule has grown to more than 280 entries, but inclusion does not provide blanket immunity from judicial review, particularly after the decisions in Waman Rao and I.R. Coelho.
21.tq: Reject the absolute claim of complete immunity and combine the numerical fact with the judicial limitation.
xs: The Ninth Schedule has grown to **more than 280** entries, but inclusion **does not confer blanket immunity** — option **(3)**.
It started with **13** Acts and now has **282**.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: **no blanket immunity**, because **judicial review is basic**; it covers land-reform laws, not only Art. 39(b), (c) laws.
xa: Its purpose: protect **land-reform/zamindari-abolition** laws from challenge for violating **Fundamental Rights**.
**Waman Rao (1981)**: entries after **24 April 1973** are open to basic-structure challenge.
Laws enter it **only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment**.

21.s: Which of the following pairs (basic feature – case) is correctly matched?
o: Rule of law – Delhi Judicial Service Association case
Independence of judiciary – P. Sambamurthy case
21.x: Bhim Singhji is associated with the welfare state; rule of law goes with P. Sambamurthy, Articles 32, 136, 141 and 142 with Delhi Judicial Service Association, and judicial independence with NJAC.
xa: **Rule of law** was also held in **Indra Sawhney (1992)**.
**Independent judiciary** also: **All India Judges Association (2002)**.
**Principle of equality**: **Indra Sawhney**; **HC powers under Arts. 226, 227**: **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**.

21.s:
Consider the following statements about basic structure cases:
1. In Kesavananda Bharati, property taxation, trade regulation and local government were associated with the basic structure.
2. The principle of secularism was reaffirmed as part of the basic structure in the All India Judges Association case.
3. L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India is associated with the basic-structure status of the powers of the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: Kesavananda Bharati associated secularism, federalism and separation of powers with the basic structure.
Statement 2: Incorrect: secularism was reaffirmed in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), decided by a nine-judge Bench.
Statement 3: Correct: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) is associated with the basic-structure status of these powers.

21.s:
Consider the following statements about the basic structure doctrine:
1. The argument that voting should be elevated beyond a statutory right is linked primarily with democracy and free and fair elections as basic features.
2. The Waman Rao judgment on the Ninth Schedule was delivered in 1981.
3. In Kesavananda Bharati, the part of Article 31C barring courts from questioning whether a law gives effect to the Directive Principles was struck down.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x:
Statement 1: Correct: the argument rests on democracy and free and fair elections being basic features of the Constitution.
Statement 2: Correct: Waman Rao came in 1981, between Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and I.R. Coelho (2007).
Statement 3: Correct: Kesavananda Bharati struck down this part of Article 31C, holding judicial review to be part of the basic structure.

21.s:
Consider the following statements about the Ninth Schedule:
1. A law can be placed in the Ninth Schedule only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment.
2. Tamil Nadu's law providing 69 per cent reservation was placed in the Ninth Schedule by the 76th Amendment Act, 1994.
3. The I.R. Coelho case applied the 'rights test' or 'direct impact test' primarily with reference to the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x:
Statement 1: Correct: inclusion needs a constitutional amendment by Parliament; the Schedule was created mainly for land-reform laws.
Statement 2: Correct: the Tamil Nadu 69 per cent reservation law was placed in the Ninth Schedule through the 76th Amendment Act, 1994.
Statement 3: Correct: a post-1973 Ninth Schedule law may be invalid if it abrogates the essence of rights under Articles 14, 19 and 21.

21.s: In which of the following cases, the Supreme Court of India enunciated the ‘Doctrine of Basic Structure’?
21.x: In the case of Keshavananda Bharti vs. the State of Kerala, (1973) a thirteen-Judge bench of the Indian Supreme Court, by a majority of 7:6, stated that the Parliament could only amend the Constitution to the extent that it did not “damage or destroy the basic structure of the Constitution” (under Article 368). Constitutional amendments are subject to judicial review; the Court essentially placed a substantive non-legislative check upon the Parliament’s power of amendment.

21.s: The Keshavananda Bharati Case is important because-
o: It sets aside the orders of the executive
The Supreme Court interpreted the basic features of
It brought the Union Government in the dock
21.x: The Supreme Court laid down the 'Basic Structure Doctrine' in the case of Keshavananda Bharati Vs State of Kerala,

21.s:
Consider the following statements about the basic structure doctrine:
1. The basic structure doctrine is judge-made, evolving case by case.
2. At present, Fundamental Rights may be amended, provided the basic structure is not damaged.
3. Eclipse, severability and pith and substance are all doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x:
Statement 1: Correct: the doctrine is not defined in the Constitution; it was developed by the Supreme Court through case law.
Statement 2: Correct: Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368, subject to the basic structure limitation.
Statement 3: Correct: eclipse, severability and pith and substance are all Supreme Court-evolved interpretive doctrines.

21.s: Which of the following is NOT a reason why the Indian Parliament is not sovereign in the British sense?
o: Parliament possesses an unlimited amending power
The Constitution is written and supreme
21.x: Parliament does not possess an unlimited amending power. The written Constitution, Fundamental Rights, judicial review, federal division of powers and limited amending power restrict parliamentary sovereignty.
21.tq: Find the option that reverses a feature of the limited constitutional system.
xs: The odd one out is "**Parliament possesses an unlimited amending power**" — option **(1)**; its amending power is in fact **limited**.
Real reasons Parliament is **not sovereign in the British sense**: **written supreme Constitution**, **FRs**, **judicial review**, **federal division** and **limited amending power**.
So options 2, 3 and 4 are genuine reasons, not exceptions.
xa: **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down **Art. 368(4), (5)**, which tried to make the amending power unlimited and non-justiciable.
Basic structure means supremacy of the **Constitution**, not of courts or Parliament.
The **42nd Amendment** gave Parliament "unlimited amending power" — it was struck down in **Minerva Mills**.

21.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 31B — Laws concerning acquisition of estates and agrarian reform
Article 31A — Acts placed in the Ninth Schedule
Article 31C — Laws implementing Article 39(b) and Article 39(c)
Article 350A — Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities
21.x: Article 31C protects laws implementing Article 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, subject to the constitutional and judicial limitations. Article 31A concerns estate acquisition and agrarian reform, Article 31B concerns Ninth Schedule laws, and Article 350B creates the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.
21.tq: Check each Article against its precise subject and identify the only correctly matched pair.
xs: **Art. 31C — laws implementing Art. 39(b), (c)** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**Art. 31C** saves such laws from **Arts. 14, 19**; it was inserted by the **25th Amendment, 1971**.
Option 1 is wrong: estates and agrarian reform belong to **Art. 31A**. Option 2 is wrong: the **Ninth Schedule** goes with **Art. 31B**.
xa: **Art. 31A** saves laws on acquisition of estates, agrarian reform from **Arts. 14, 19** — inserted by the **1st Amendment, 1951**.
The **Ninth Schedule** was created by the **1st Amendment (1951)** with **Art. 31B**.
⚠ Kesavananda struck down the part of **Art. 31C** that barred courts from questioning a law declared to give effect to DPSP.

21.s:
Consider the following statements about the basic structure doctrine:
1. The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied by the Supreme Court of India in Golaknath (1967).
2. The basic structure doctrine primarily rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review by the courts.
3. The restriction imposed by the 42nd Amendment on High Courts' power to review central laws was removed by the 39th Amendment Act, 1975.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x:
Statement 1: Correct: prospective overruling is a judge-made doctrine first applied in Golaknath (1967).
Statement 2: Correct: the doctrine rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the courts' power to review amendments.
Statement 3: Incorrect: the restriction was removed by the 43rd Amendment Act, 1977, not the 39th.

21.s:
Assertion (A): The basic structure doctrine has been criticised as judicial rewriting of the Constitution.
Reason (R): The doctrine has no explicit textual definition and its content is developed by unelected judges case by case.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
21.x: Both statements are true. The absence of a textual definition and the open-ended judicial development of the doctrine form the basis of this criticism.
21.tq: Check whether the reason directly explains the criticism stated in the assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
A is true: critics call the doctrine a "**rewriting of the Constitution**" by **unelected judges**.
R is true and explains A: it has **no textual basis** and its **list is open-ended**, so its content is uncertain.
xa: Critics also call it "**judicial supremacy**"; it is described as **vague and unlisted**.
Defence: it is among the **biggest contributions of the Indian judiciary** to constitutionalism.
Supporters call it the Constitution's **shield against majorities**.

21.s: Which of the following statements regarding the debate on the 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, is correct?
o: The Supreme Court struck down the Bill for violating judicial independence.
Former CJI B.R. Gavai stated before the JPC that the Bill did not violate the basic structure, while U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna raised doubts.
Former CJI B.R. Gavai stated that simultaneous polls necessarily violate the basic structure.
Former CJIs U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna rejected all basic-structure concerns about simultaneous polls.
21.x: B.R. Gavai told the Joint Parliamentary Committee that the 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, did not violate the basic structure, whereas former Chief Justices U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna raised basic-structure doubts.
21.tq: Match each public position with the correct constitutional office-holder.
xs: Ex-CJI **B.R. Gavai** told the **JPC** the **129th Amendment Bill, 2024** does **not** violate basic structure, while **U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna** raised doubts — option **(2)**.
The Bill concerns **simultaneous polls**; it has not been struck down by the Supreme Court.
Options 3 and 4 reverse the views of Gavai and of Lalit and Khanna.
xa: Basic structure = what **cannot be amended** under **Art. 368**.
**Free and fair elections** and **federalism** are among the listed basic features.
Critics call the doctrine **vague and unlisted**, even "**judicial supremacy**".

21.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Judicial Review is an inherent power of constitutional courts.
II. Judicial Review examines legislative enactments and executive actions for constitutional validity.
III. Basic structural features may be destroyed through Article 368.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x: I and II are correct: judicial review is an inherent power of constitutional courts to test laws and executive action. III is false because the basic structure cannot be destroyed even under Article 368.
21.tq: Find the statement that contradicts the Basic Structure Doctrine.
n: Judicial Review is an inherent power of constitutional courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Judicial Review examines legislative enactments against constitutional validity. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Judicial Review examines executive actions against constitutional validity. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Core structural features of the Constitution cannot be abrogated or destroyed even through Article 368. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xs: Statements **I and II** are correct — so option **(1) I and II only** is correct.
I and II: **Judicial Review** is an **inherent power** of constitutional courts to examine **legislative enactments** and **executive actions**.
III is wrong: per **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, core features **cannot be abrogated or destroyed**, even through **Article 368**.
xa: ⚠ Basic Structure is **not** defined in **Part XX** — it is **judge-made**.
The idea came from **Germany** (Basic Law); jurist **Dietrich Conrad** argued for **implied limits**.
First applied in **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)**.
**Waman Rao (1981)**: cut-off date **24 April 1973**.

21.s:
Consider the following statements about the basic structure doctrine:
1. Under the basic structure doctrine, Parliament may amend every constitutional provision without limitation.
2. The Preamble alone constitutes the basic structure.
3. Secularism did not become a basic feature only because of its textual insertion in 1976.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
21.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: Parliament may amend the Constitution but cannot damage or destroy its core features.
Statement 2: Incorrect: the Preamble is part of the Constitution and amendable subject to the basic structure, which is not confined to the Preamble.
Statement 3: Correct: secularism was treated as a basic feature even before the 42nd Amendment added the word 'secular' to the Preamble.

21.s: The Supreme Court of India has propounded the ‘Doctrine of Basic Structure’ of the Constitution in which of the following cases?
21.x: The doctrine of the basic structure of the Constitution owes its evolution to the majority judgment of the Supreme Court in the landmark case, Keshvananda Bharati Vs. State of Kerala (1973), which was approved in Minerva Mills Vs. Union of India (1980) case.

21.s: Which one of the following cases outlined the basic structure doctrine of the Indian Constitution?
Which one of the following cases propounded the concept of ‘Basic structure’ of the Indian Constitution?
The Supreme Court of India enunciated the doctrine of ‘Basic Structure of the Constitution’ in
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Free and fair elections — Minerva Mills
High Court powers under Articles 226 and 227 — S.R. Bommai
21.x: B is correct: Indra Sawhney (1992) is listed for the principle of equality. Free and fair elections go with Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (and Kuldip Nayar), not Minerva Mills; HC powers under Arts. 226-227 with L. Chandra Kumar (1997), not S.R. Bommai; independent judiciary with All India Judges Association and the NJAC case, not Waman Rao.
21.tq: Use the case-specific association and watch for swapped case names.
xs: **Principle of equality — Indra Sawhney** is correctly matched — option **(2)**.
**Free and fair elections** go with **Raj Narain (1975)** and **Kuldip Nayar (2006)**, not Minerva Mills.
**HC powers under Arts. 226, 227** go with **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**, not S.R. Bommai; **independent judiciary** with **All India Judges Association** and **NJAC**, not Waman Rao.
xa: **Indra Sawhney (1992)** is also cited for **rule of law**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)**: **secularism** and **federalism**.
**Waman Rao (1981)**: Ninth Schedule cut-off **24 April 1973**.

21.s: The source of the ‘Basic Structure Theory of the Constitution’ in India is
21.x: The Parliament could not use its amending powers under Article 368 to ‘damage,’ destroy,’ ‘abrogate,’ change’ or alter the ‘basic structure’ or framework of the Constitution. The view expressed in the Keshavananda Bharati Case was subsequently approved in the Minerva Mills' Case, 1980.

21.s: The basic structure theory of the Constitution of India implies that –
o: Certain features of the Constitution are so essential to
Fundamental rights cannot be abridged or taken away
The Constitution cannot be amended except in
The Preamble of the Constitution cannot be amended
21.x: The basic structure theory of the Constitution of India implies that certain features of the Constitution are so essential to it that they cannot be abrogated. The Supreme Court made it clear in its judgment in the case of Keshavananda Bharati Vs State of Kerala, 1973, that there are certain basic features of the Constitution which cannot be amended in any case.

21.s: Coelho case is related to which Schedule of the Constitution of India?
21.x: The Coelho case is a landmark case which upheld the authority of the Judiciary to review laws - including those under the 9th schedule - against violation of the Basic structure of the constitution. It is also known as the 9th schedule case.

22.s:
Consider the following statements about foundational Supreme Court cases:
1. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India laid down that the right to travel abroad is exclusively a statutory right.
2. Shayara Bano v. Union of India is associated with the compulsory registration of marriages.
3. The Supreme Court judgment confining handcuffing to exceptional cases is associated with Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
22.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: Maneka Gandhi held that Article 21 includes dignity and travel abroad and requires a just, fair and reasonable procedure.
Statement 2: Incorrect: compulsory registration of marriages was directed in Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006).

22.s: Which statement correctly describes ADM Jabalpur (1976)?
o: It struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act.
It held that Fundamental Rights, including Article 21, were unenforceable during Emergency.
It held that Article 21 remained fully enforceable during Emergency.

22.x: ADM Jabalpur held that Fundamental Rights, including Article 21, could not be enforced during the Emergency. The reasoning was later effectively overruled and rejected in Puttaswamy.
22.tq: Discriminate between a discredited earlier ruling and the later judgment that rejected it.
xs: **ADM Jabalpur (1976)** held **FRs incl. Art. 21 unenforceable in Emergency** — option **(2)**.
It is called the "**darkest day**" and has been **effectively overruled**; **Puttaswamy** rejected its reasoning.
**Sec. 66A** fell in **Shreya Singhal (2015)**; privacy came in **Puttaswamy (2017)**.
xa: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: Art. 21 procedure must be **fair, just and reasonable**.
**Andrabi v NIA (18 May 2026)**: **bail is the rule** even under the **UAPA**.
Puttaswamy: **nine judges**, CJI **J.S. Khehar**.

22.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: A.K. Gopalan gave a narrow interpretation of Article 21.
Berubari Union held that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.
S.R. Bommai laid guidelines against arbitrary misuse of Article 356.
Champakam Dorairajan held that Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs in case of conflict.
22.x: Option B is incorrect: Berubari Union (1960) held that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution. Kesavananda Bharati later held that it is.
n: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras gave Article 21 a narrow interpretation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Berubari Union Case held that the Preamble is not an integral part of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India laid down guidelines against arbitrary misuse of Article 356. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Champakam Dorairajan held that Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles of State Policy in case of conflict. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **Berubari Union** held the **Preamble** an integral part — option **(2)**.
**Berubari Union (1960)** held the Preamble **not** an integral part; overturned by **Kesavananda Bharati** and **S.R. Bommai**.
**A.K. Gopalan** gave a **narrow** reading of **Article 21**; **S.R. Bommai** set guidelines on **Article 356**; **Champakam** held FRs **prevail over** DPSP.
xa: **Berubari** is linked to **Article 3** and the Preamble.
**Champakam (1951)** led to the **First Amendment, 1951** and **Article 15(4)**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)** was a **Nine-judge** bench.

22.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: P. Sambamurthy – 52nd Amendment and the Tenth Schedule
Champakam Dorairajan – Fundamental Rights prevailing over DPSPs
A.K. Gopalan – Preventive detention and procedure established by law

22.x: P. Sambamurthy concerned judicial review and special provisions for Andhra Pradesh; the Tenth Schedule case is Kihoto Hollohan.
n: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras focused on “procedure established by law”. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras concerned preventive detention. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Champakam Dorairajan held that Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles of State Policy in case of conflict. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]

xa: **P. Sambamurthy (1987)** struck down portions of the **32nd Amendment**.
**Raj Narain (1975)** held **free and fair elections** part of the Basic Structure.

22.s:
Consider the following statements about foundational Supreme Court cases:
1. The 'golden triangle' involving Articles 14, 19 and 21 was established in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras.
2. Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain is linked to the 39th Amendment.
3. The Berubari Union case did not hold that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.

22.s:
Consider the following statements about foundational Supreme Court cases:
1. The Berubari Union case was decided in 1960.
2. The 39th Constitutional Amendment was nullified by the 42nd Amendment.
3. The Berubari Union case dealt with Article 3 and the Preamble.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
22.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Berubari was 1960, after Shankari Prasad (1951) and before Sajjan Singh (1965).
Statement 2: Incorrect: the 44th Amendment (1978), not the 42nd, undid the 39th Amendment's changes.

22.s:
Assertion (A): Indira Nehru Gandhi treated free and fair elections as part of the Basic Structure.

n: Indira Nehru Gandhi struck down parts of the 39th Constitutional Amendment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]

22.s:
Consider the following statements about headline Supreme Court cases:
1. The Minerva Mills case made President's Rule under Article 356 subject to judicial review and emphasised the floor test.
2. The Vishaka Guidelines were issued because workplace sexual harassment was held to violate the constitutional guarantees of equality and life.
3. In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court held that privacy is a statutory right but not a fundamental right.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
22.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: it was the nine-judge S.R. Bommai judgment that made Article 356 reviewable and stressed the floor test.
Statement 2: Correct: Vishaka treated workplace sexual harassment as a violation of equality and life.
Statement 3: Incorrect: Puttaswamy recognised privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21.

22.s:

A. Vishaka
B. Shreya Singhal
C. S.R. Bommai
D. K.S. Puttaswamy
22.x: S.R. Bommai was decided in 1994, Vishaka in 1997, Shreya Singhal in 2015 and K.S. Puttaswamy in 2017.
22.tq: Anchor the earliest and latest years, then arrange the middle judgments.
xs: Order **C, A, B, D** — option **(1)**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)** → **Vishaka (1997)** → **Shreya Singhal (2015)** → **K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)**.
xa: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** and **Minerva Mills (1980)** come before all four.
**Indra Sawhney (1992)** precedes Bommai.

Minerva Mills — Fundamental Rights and DPSP are complementary

xs: **S.R. Bommai — Abolition of untouchability** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.

**Indra Sawhney** — **50% ceiling, creamy layer**; **Minerva Mills** — FRs and DPSP **complementary**: both correct.

Statement 1: Correct: Naz Foundation (Delhi High Court, 2009) first read down Section 377; Navtej Singh Johar followed in 2018.

1. In Supriyo v. Union of India (October 2023), the Supreme Court left the issue of same-sex marriage to the State Legislatures.
2. Lalita Kumari (2013) made registration of an FIR mandatory for cognizable offences.
3. The Shah Bano case (1985) struck down Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act.

22.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: Supriyo held there is no fundamental right to marry and left same-sex marriage to Parliament, not the State Legislatures.
Statement 2: Correct: Lalita Kumari made FIR registration mandatory under Section 154 CrPC (now Section 173 BNSS).
Statement 3: Incorrect: Shah Bano concerned maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC and called for a Uniform Civil Code.

22.s:
Consider the following statements about Supreme Court election-law judgments:
1. Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act was struck down in Lily Thomas (2013).
2. In Union of India v. ADR (2002), the Supreme Court required election candidates to disclose their criminal record, assets and educational qualifications.
3. The Anoop Baranwal committee for selecting the CEC and Election Commissioners was to operate only until Parliament made a law.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
22.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Lily Thomas (2013) concerned the disqualification of convicted legislators and struck down Section 8(4).
Statement 2: Correct: the ADR judgment required disclosure of criminal record, assets and educational qualifications.
Statement 3: Correct: the Court's committee was to operate only until Parliament made a law, which Parliament did in 2023.

1. Lily Thomas (2013) held that convicted MPs and MLAs could continue in office until their appeals were finally decided.
2. PUCL (2013) led to the introduction of the NOTA option on EVMs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
22.x: Statement 2 is correct: PUCL (2013) brought the NOTA option on EVMs. Statement 1 is wrong: Lily Thomas (2013) struck down Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act, so convicted MPs and MLAs are disqualified at once. So '2 only'.
22.tq: 2013: PUCL = NOTA; Lily Thomas = Sec 8(4) RPA struck down.
xs: Only statement **2** is correct — so option **(1) 2 only** is correct.
2: **PUCL (2013)** brought the **NOTA** option on EVMs.
1 is wrong: **Lily Thomas (2013)** struck down **Sec. 8(4) RPA** — convicted MPs/MLAs are **disqualified at once**.
xa: ⚠ **PUCL** and **Lily Thomas** both **2013** = NOTA vs Sec. 8(4) RPA.
**Union of India v. ADR (2002)**: candidates must disclose **criminal record, assets, education**.
**Anoop Baranwal (2023)**: CEC/ECs chosen by **PM, LoP, CJI** till a law is made.

1. In the December 2023 Article 370 judgment, the Supreme Court treated Article 370 as a temporary provision.
2. Visakhapatnam became the sole capital of Andhra Pradesh with effect from 2 June 2024, and the Supreme Court approved three capitals.
3. Javed (2003) held that polygamy is not an essential religious practice.

22.s:

1. Articles 32, 141 and 142 are significant in the context of Vishaka and Seema because they enable the Supreme Court to fill legislative gaps temporarily until Parliament acts.
2. NALSA v. Union of India recognised transgender individuals as the Third Gender.
3. Minerva Mills struck down the IMDT Act for breaching the Union's duty under Article 355.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

Statement 2: Correct: NALSA (2014) recognised transgender people as a third gender with the right to self-identify their gender.
Statement 3: Incorrect: the IMDT Act was struck down in Sarbananda Sonowal (2005), not Minerva Mills, for breaching Article 355.

With reference to the Aadhaar judgment (Puttaswamy II, 2018), consider the following statements:
1. Section 57 of the Aadhaar Act was struck down, so private entities cannot demand Aadhaar on that basis.
2. Authentication records may be retained for a maximum of three months.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
22.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the limit is six months, not three months (the three-month version is the UPSC trap). Statement 1 is correct: Section 57 was struck down, so private entities cannot demand or use Aadhaar data on that basis. So '1 only'.

xa: The Aadhaar Act was upheld **4:1** with limits.
Aadhaar is mandatory for **subsidies from the Consolidated Fund** and **PAN/ITR**.
Not mandatory for **bank accounts**, **SIMs**, **school admissions**, exams.
Aadhaar does **not prove citizenship, domicile or date of birth** (**Sec. 9**).

Statement 3: Incorrect: the proposition was associated with Andrabi v. NIA (reported on 18 May 2026), not S.R. Bommai.

22.s: 'Right to Privacy' is protected under which Article of the Constitution of India?
22.x: The Right to Privacy is protected under Article 21 of the Constitution of India, which guarantees the Right to Life and Personal Liberty. This was affirmed by the Supreme Court in the landmark Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India judgment (2017), where a nine-judge bench unanimously held that the Right to Privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21 and is also connected with the freedoms guaranteed under other fundamental rights.

22.s: Under which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India, has the Supreme Court of India placed the Right to Privacy?
22.x: In 2012, Justice K. S. Puttaswamy, a retired High Court judge, filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court challenging the constitutional validity of the Aadhaar scheme introduced by the UPA Government. Initially assigned to a Five-Judge Bench, the matter was later referred to a Nine-Judge Bench. In a landmark decision on August 24, 2017, the Bench unanimously recognised the fundamental right to privacy for every individual, as Indian Polity: Constitutional Framework PMF IAS IP – 11 guaranteed by the Constitution, specifically within Article 21 (Protection of Life and Personal Liberty) and Part III as a whole. The right to privacy is also enshrined in Article 17 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which India is a party.

o: Golaknath Vs. The State of Punjab

22.s: Under which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India, has the Supreme Court of India placed the Right to Privacy?
22.x: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) & Anr. vs. Union of India and Ors. case, the Nine-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in a landmark judgement on 24 August, 2017 unanimously ruled that privacy is a fundamental right, and that the right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty (Article 21), as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.

22.s: Right to Privacy is contained in:
22.x: Article-21 The Right to Privacy has been held to be a part of the Right to Life and Personal Liberty under Article 21. This was affirmed by the Supreme Court in the landmark K.S. Puttaswamy judgment (2017). The ruling recognised privacy as a fundamental right implicit within the broader guarantee of Article 21.

22.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Statement-I: The Supreme Court of India has held in some judgements that the reservation policies made under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India would be limited by Article 335 for maintenance of efficiency of administration.
2. Statement-II: Article 335 of the Constitution of India defines the term 'efficiency of administration'. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, and Statement-II is the correct
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, and Statement-II is not the correct
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
22.x: Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect: The Supreme Court of India has consistently referred to the notions of "efficiency" and "merit" while adjudicating the validity of various reservation policies. The Court has held in several judgments — Indra Sawhney v Union of India 1993; M Nagaraj v Union of India 2006 — that the reservation policies made under Article 16 (4) of the Constitution would be limited by Article 335, which provides for "maintenance of efficiency of administration," while considering the claims of the Scheduled Castes (SCs) and the Scheduled Tribes (STs) in the making of appointments to public services and posts. This was done while the Constitution does not define the term "efficiency of administration. "This gap in interpretation was filled by a twojudge bench in the B K Pavitra (II) v Union of India (2019), as it held that "efficiency of adminis­tration in the affairs of the union or of a state must be defined in an inclusive sense, where diverse segments of society find representation as a true aspiration of governance by and for the people." Indian Polity: Organs of the State PMF IAS IP – 83 PMF Concept Hack: Statement II is clearly wrong because the Constitution often mentions concepts without clearly defining them. Article 335 refers to "efficiency of administration" but does not define it. Hence, Statement II is incorrect, making option (c) the correct answer.

22.s: Right to Privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of Right to Life and Personal Liberty. Which of the following in the Constitution of India correctly and appropriately imply the above statement?
o: Article 14 and the provisions under the 42nd
Article 17 and the Directive Principles of State Policy
Article 21 and the freedoms guaranteed in Part III
Article 24 and the provisions under the 44th
22.x: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) and others. Vs. Union of India, is a landmark judgment of the Supreme Court of India, which holds that the Right to Privacy is protected as a Fundamental Right under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. Hence, Option (c) is correct.

22.s: Which of the following Article/Articles read with the word ‘Socialist’ used in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution enabled the Supreme Court to deduce a fundamental right to Equal Pay for Equal Work?
22.x: In a landmark case of Randhir Singh Vs. Union of India, the Supreme Court held that "Construing Article 14 and 16 in the light of the preamble and Article 39 (d) we are of the view that the principle 'Equal pay for equal work' is deducible from those Articles and may be properly applied to cases of unequal scales of pay based on no classification or irrational classification though these drawing the different scales of pay do identical work under the same employer." Thus correct answer is option (d).
